english.html: of himself, of his posterity and of such tyrants, hanged with his feet uppermost and his head hanging over the river Pactolus, whose sand is of gold. Which Ovid eloquently expresses when he says <sup class="mk" data-key="e">e</sup>:

notes.citation: Ovid, Ibis, lines 299–300 (the numbering varies by edition)
notes.gloss: Morte vel intereas capti suspensus Achaei, / qui miser aurifera teste pependit aqua: the print's Onide is Ouide, and its reſte is the editions' teste.

english.html: Or may you perish by the death of captive Achaeus, hanged, who, wretched, hung by a rope over the gold-bearing water (Morte vel intereas, capti suspensus Achaei, Qui miser aurifera reste pependit aqua).

And in the books of the Roman Pontiffs it was ordained, among other things, that the bodies of the hanged, as abominable, should have no burial, but should be, as in disdain, thrown upon the ground, to be eaten and devoured by birds, dogs and other famished beasts.

Rigour would certainly have commanded that he be burnt alive <sup class="mk" data-key="a">a</sup>; but to obviate some despair which might have overcome the temerity of this impostor, frantic and full of rage, the Court ordered that he should first be strangled. Wherein all judges shall be admonished not to exercise, without some great and notable cause, those cruel and brutal ferocities of burning or dismembering malefactors while fully alive. In which carnage, nevertheless, some who are bloodthirsty, inhumanly unnatural, and born, as it seems, to all rigour and ferocity, take such pleasure that one would never see them at ease or content except when they have thus fought against nature, and cruelly shed, by new and unheard-of punishments, the blood of their neighbour: and sometimes so furiously that the most barbarous and cruel tyrants would have horror of performing like acts. Which proceeds most often from a brutal nature, but sometimes from ignorance or from wickedness: for (besides that

notes.citation: Digest 48.13.7 (Ad legem Iuliam peculatus et de sacrilegis, l. Sacrilegii, Ulpian)
notes.original: l. ſacrilegij. D. ad l. Iul. pe cul.
notes.gloss: The proconsul fixes the penalty of sacrilege by the quality of the person and the circumstances: many have condemned the sacrilegious to the beasts, some have burnt them alive (vivos exussisse), others hanged them on the fork. Cited again at {h}.

english.html: Than an unskilled man, nothing is ever more unjust (Homine imperito nunquam quicquam iniustius) b),

notes.gloss: Homine imperito numquam quicquam iniustius, / qui nisi quod ipse fecit nil rectum putat: nothing is more unjust than an ignorant man, who thinks nothing right but what he has done himself.

english.html: just as the unskilled, under this pretext, think to cover their imperfection and ignorance, so the wicked also believe
